questions.q: What makes diffusion alone insufficient for large multicellular organisms?
questions.a: Deep inside a big body, every cell is too far from the surface, so diffusion would be too slow to supply all needs.

questions.q: Why do organisms need maintenance of their bodies?
questions.a: Tissues wear out and break; energy and materials are needed continuously to repair and keep life processes going.

questions.q: What raw materials do living things take from outside?
questions.a: Food (organic molecules), oxygen, water and minerals - sources of energy and building material.

questions.q: Define autotrophic nutrition.
questions.a: An organism builds its own food from simple inorganic substances like CO2 and water using sunlight and chlorophyll, as green plants do.

questions.q: Write the overall events of photosynthesis.
questions.a: Chlorophyll traps light energy, water splits to release oxygen, and carbon dioxide is reduced to carbohydrate.

questions.q: Why do land plants take in CO2 through stomata at night too?
questions.a: Stomata must open for gas exchange but opening loses water, so CO2 intake is timed and balanced against water loss.

questions.q: What is heterotrophic nutrition? Name its main types.
questions.a: Depending on other organisms for food: holozoic (animals), saprotrophic (fungi on dead matter) and parasitic (like cuscuta, tapeworm).

questions.q: How does a parasite like cuscuta feed?
questions.a: It draws ready-made food from the host plant through sucking roots, lacking chlorophyll of its own.

questions.q: Give one example each of a parasite and a saprotroph.
questions.a: Parasite: tapeworm (or cuscuta); saprotroph: bread mould or mushroom growing on decaying matter.

questions.q: Name the main parts of the human alimentary canal in order.
questions.a: Mouth, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine and anus, with liver and pancreas adding secretions.

questions.q: What happens to food in the small intestine?
questions.a: Bile emulsifies fats, pancreatic enzymes digest all food types, and villi absorb the digested nutrients into blood.

questions.q: Why do we chew food thoroughly?
questions.a: Teeth break food small, saliva mixes and its amylase starts starch digestion, easing later steps.

questions.q: What is the fate of glucose in aerobic respiration?
questions.a: It breaks fully into carbon dioxide and water in mitochondria, releasing a lot of energy.

questions.q: Where does anaerobic respiration occur in human muscle and what forms?
questions.a: In muscle cells during heavy exercise when oxygen is short, glucose becomes lactic acid, causing cramps.

questions.q: Why is energy release larger in aerobic respiration?
questions.a: Complete breakdown of glucose in the presence of oxygen releases far more energy than partial breakdown without it.

solution_steps.explain: 1 mol of ATP on hydrolysis releases about 30.5 kJ

questions.a: 21.869 kcal

concepts.title: Human Respiratory System and Gas Exchange

questions.q: How is oxygen carried from lungs to tissues?
questions.a: The respiratory pigment haemoglobin in red blood cells binds oxygen and releases it at tissues.

questions.q: Why are alveoli thin-walled and rich in blood vessels?
questions.a: Thin walls shorten the diffusion path and rich blood supply quickly carries away oxygen, speeding gas exchange.

questions.q: What mechanism moves air in and out of human lungs?
questions.a: The rib muscles and diaphragm change chest volume and pressure, drawing air in and pushing it out.

questions.q: Why is the human heart called a double pump?
questions.a: Its right half pumps blood to the lungs and the left half pumps oxygenated blood to the whole body - two circuits in one organ.

questions.q: Why do ventricles have thicker walls than atria?
questions.a: Ventricles must push blood to distant organs (or lungs) at higher pressure; atria only fill ventricles.

questions.q: What are valves in the heart for?
questions.a: They stop blood from flowing backwards, keeping it moving in one direction.

questions.q: How does water rise to the top of a tall tree?
questions.a: Root pressure pushes water upward and transpiration pull from leaf evaporation draws the water column up the xylem.

questions.q: What does the phloem transport and in what form?
questions.a: Food made in leaves is carried as sucrose solution to storage and growth parts - called translocation.

questions.q: Why does loss of water from leaves help the plant?
questions.a: It creates the suction pull that lifts water and minerals, and cools the plant.

concepts.title: Human Excretory System and Nephron Function

questions.q: Name the basic filtration unit of the kidney.
questions.a: The nephron, a coiled tubule with a cup-shaped Bowman's capsule around a glomerulus.

questions.q: What is reabsorbed in the nephron tubule?
questions.a: Useful substances - glucose, amino acids, most salts and much water - pass back into blood from the filtrate.

questions.q: Why do we pass only 1-2 L of urine a day though 180 L is filtered?
questions.a: Nearly 99% of the filtrate is reabsorbed; only the concentrated wastes leave as urine.

solution_steps.name: filtrate_per_hour
solution_steps.explain: the kidneys filter about 180 L of blood daily, so divide by 24

solution_steps.name: reabsorbed_volume
solution_steps.explain: almost all the filtrate is reabsorbed; only urine is excreted

questions.q: The kidneys form 180 L of filtrate per day and excrete 1.4 L of urine. How much is reabsorbed, and what per cent of the filtrate is that?
A patient's kidneys filter 180 L daily and pass 1.5 L of urine. Find the reabsorbed volume and its percentage.
If 180 L of filtrate leads to only 1.2 L of urine, how many litres are reabsorbed and what per cent is reabsorbed?
Daily filtrate is 180 L and urine output is exactly 1 L. Compute reabsorption in litres and in per cent.
With 180 L filtrate and 2 L urine in a day, what volume is reabsorbed and what per cent does that represent?
How do plants get rid of their wastes?
questions.a: Waste products diffuse into surrounding water, collect in old leaves which fall, or leave as resins and gums in old xylem.

questions.q: What plant waste is stored in leaves that fall in autumn?
questions.a: Toxic wastes and by-products are parked in leaves and shed with them.

questions.q: Name two substances excreted by plants that humans use.
questions.a: Resins and gums (also essential oils and rubber) - plant excretory products useful to us.
